quote: und wie kann man eine algebraische Fläche solcher Art finden?
english: And how can one find an algebraic surface of this kind?
topic: The page ends a note on a surface problem with a reference to Bianchi's theorem that fundamental quantities determine a surface, then asks whether a fixed family of closed curves bounds the true convergence region of expansions in a given series of analytic functions, and closes with questions inspired by Boy's surface: a 3-dimensional image of projective space in 4-space, and surfaces having a prescribed space curve as double curve.

triage.modern_statement: In context (questions prompted by Boy's surface), the most likely reading is: find an explicit real algebraic surface in R^3 (a polynomial equation or polynomial/rational parametrization) that realizes an immersion of the real projective plane of Boy's type. That means a surface whose only singularities are self-intersections along double curves (plus a triple point), with no pinch points/cusps, unlike the Steiner Roman surface and the cross-cap. An alternative reading, which the note's wording leaves open, is: construct an algebraic surface that has a given space curve as its double curve.
triage.answered_by: For the Boy's-surface reading: Werner Boy found the immersion in 1901 as Hilbert's doctoral student, but only topologically and without equations. Bernard Morin gave the first explicit parametrization in 1978. François Apéry gave an algebraic realization in 1986: Boy's surface is the real zero set of a degree-6 polynomial, a sextic. Morin and Apéry (1987) also gave a family of parametrizations running from the Roman surface to Boy's surface. I found no source that addresses the alternative 'prescribed double curve' reading.

evidence.claim: Boy's surface is an immersion of the real projective plane in 3-space, found by Werner Boy in 1901. Hilbert, his thesis advisor, had asked him to prove that such an immersion could not exist.

Boy's surface came out of the search for a model of the projective plane whose only singularities are self-intersections. The previously known models, the Roman surface and the cross-cap, have cuspidal points. The page lists Apéry's 1986 Cartesian parametrization and the Morin–Apéry 1987 family, and calls the result an algebraic surface of degree 6.
Boy's surface can be realized as a real algebraic variety of degree six, while a Steiner surface has degree at most four.
F. Apéry defines Boy's surface as the real zero set of a degree-six polynomial and gives a parametrization of its self-intersection curve.
Boy's surface can be described implicitly by a sextic polynomial.

triage.why: The page's context (Boy's surface, double curves) strongly suggests Hilbert wanted an algebraic model of Boy's immersion of RP^2. Boy's 1901 construction was purely topological. Sources agree that an algebraic sextic realization was found later: Morin's 1978 parametrization, Apéry's 1986 work, and Morin–Apéry 1987. This is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Confidence is medium rather than high for two reasons. First, 'solcher Art' could refer instead to surfaces with a prescribed double curve, and I found no source that tracks that reading. Second, the citations come from secondary web pages, and I did not check Apéry's original papers directly.
